Wilkinson, R.H. (2003). The Complete Gods and Goddesses of Ancient Egypt.

egy.solar_gold_palette.name: Solar Gold Palette
egy.solar_gold_palette.summary: A warm solar palette centred on gold, amber, and yellow ochre accented by deep lapis blue — evoking the sun, divine golden flesh, and celestial light of Egyptian solar theology.
egy.solar_gold_palette.description: The solar gold palette is anchored in the Egyptian theological identity of gold as the flesh of the gods and the substance of the sun's light. Used for divine figures (especially solar deities — Ra, Amun-Ra, Khepri, Aten), royal jewellery contexts, and luminous funerary art. The palette pairs warm gold and amber tones with deep lapis lazuli blue as the celestial contrast, following the actual combinations found in royal jewellery (Tutankhamun's pectorals, for example). Carbon black outlines and white calcite highlights complete the system. This palette is the most festive and luminous of the Egyptian colour systems — appropriate for divine enthronement, solar barque, and celestial ceiling contexts.

do: Lead with warm gold (#C8922A–#D4A82A) as the dominant warm tone.
Contrast with deep lapis blue (#1A3A6B–#2A5B9A) as the celestial cool.
Use carbon black for outline and deep shadow.
Include calcite white for sky/light highlights.
avoid: Avoid cool yellows (lemon yellow) — use only warm amber-gold range.
Avoid mixing saturated red or green as primaries — gold and lapis are the stars.

Aldred, C. (1971). Jewels of the Pharaohs. Thames and Hudson.

egy.sphinx.name: Sphinx
egy.sphinx.summary: The composite creature with lion body and human (or ram or falcon) head — a symbol of royal power, solar guardianship, and the liminal threshold between worlds.
egy.sphinx.description: The sphinx is the classic Egyptian composite being: the power of the lion combined with the intelligence and divinity of the human head (androsphinx), ram head (criosphinx, associated with Amun), or falcon head (hieracosphinx, associated with Horus). The Great Sphinx at Giza (c. 2500 BCE) is the most famous example — a colossal limestone androsphinx wearing the nemes headdress, facing east to receive the sunrise. Sphinxes appear as avenue figures lining processional routes to temples (criosphinx avenues at Karnak), as tomb guardians, on amulets, and in relief. The recumbent pose (paws extended, body flat) is canonical. The hieracosphinx appears frequently on royal jewellery (pectorals). Compositionally, paired sphinxes frame an entrance or central emblem as heraldic guardians.

do: Use recumbent pose (lion body lying down, paws forward) as canonical form.
Include nemes headdress for androsphinx royal identification.
Pair as bilateral guardians flanking entrance or central emblem.
avoid: Avoid standing or crouching poses — the recumbent form is definitively Egyptian.
Avoid winged variants (more Greek-style) without clear remix/period labelling.

Wilkinson, R.H. (1992). Reading Egyptian Art. Thames and Hudson.

egy.stone_surface_texture.name: Egyptian Stone Surface Texture
egy.stone_surface_texture.summary: The characteristic surface qualities of carved Egyptian stonework — limestone, sandstone, and granite — with their grain, colour, and weathering profiles for digital simulation.
egy.stone_surface_texture.description:
Egyptian monumental art is primarily executed in three stone types, each with distinct surface characteristics:
1. Limestone: The most common medium for tomb and temple relief in the Memphis
   region (Giza, Saqqara). Cream-to-warm-white base colour; fine grain;
   excellent for shallow relief carving; weathers to warm ochre with dust patina.
   Nummulitic limestone (with visible fossil inclusions) is characteristic of
   Giza blocks.

2. Sandstone: Dominant in Upper Egypt (Luxor, Karnak, Edfu, Aswan). Warm ochre-
   to-buff colour; coarser grain than limestone; suitable for deeply cut relief;
   slightly friable surface. Nubian sandstone (brown-red) at Aswan and Nubian sites.

3. Granite (red/grey): Used for statuary, obelisks, sarcophagi, and high-wear
   architectural elements. Deep red-pink (Aswan red granite) or grey-blue;
   crystalline grain visible at close range; highly resistant to weathering.

Surface aging: all three stone types develop dust/calcium patina in desert conditions; limestone erodes more quickly than sandstone; granite retains sharpness the longest. Modern conservation treatments (consolidants) can give an artificially bright surface.

do: Warm the base colour: limestone = cream/ochre, sandstone = buff/amber, granite = red-pink.
Add dust patina and edge wear as default aging simulation.
Use directional side-lighting to read carved surface as relief.
avoid: Avoid cold grey stone colour — Egyptian stone is almost always warm-toned.
Avoid over-polished surfaces for relief work — most Egyptian stone carving is matte.

sources: Nicholson, P.T. & Shaw, I. (eds.) (2000). Ancient Egyptian Materials and Technology. Cambridge University Press.

egy.street_poster_remix.name: Street Poster / Screen Print Remix
egy.street_poster_remix.summary: A bold, high-contrast remix placing Egyptian canonical figures and symbols in the visual language of screen print, linocut, or propaganda poster design — using limited flat colour, heavy ink, and typographic overlays.
egy.street_poster_remix.description:
This remix channels the poster and print traditions — Soviet constructivism, WPA prints, Shepard Fairey-style stencil work, and risograph zine culture — to create large-format statement pieces grounded in Egyptian visual language. The "historical-first" base: canonical profile figures, register composition, and authentic motifs. The remix layer: dramatic flat-colour reduction (2–4 inks), heavy grain texture from screen print halftone or risograph raster, bold slab- serif or condensed display type, and oversized motifs that bleed to the edge.
Colour palette options: - 2-colour: black + ochre gold (most powerful) - 3-colour: black + ochre + turquoise - 4-colour: full split-fountain or risograph CMYK-adjacent
The grammar: Egyptian register structures become horizontal poster divisions; scale hierarchy drives the primary focal point; hieroglyphic-inspired marks fill border bands as texture (not text). The result reads as a political poster but with an ancient Egyptian soul.

do: Reduce to 2–4 flat ink colours — screen print discipline.
Apply coarse halftone or risograph grain texture for print authenticity.
Maintain Egyptian canonical figure proportions even in simplified form.
Include bold typographic element (title, phrase) using period-adjacent slab or condensed type.
avoid: Avoid photorealism — screen print is flat, graphic, and high-contrast.
Avoid more than 4 inks unless specifically targeting full-colour poster look.
Avoid fake hieroglyphic text in the typographic elements.

egy.street_poster_remix.prompt_fragment: "Egyptian screen print poster remix, 2-3 flat colour inks, black and gold ochre, risograph grain texture, canonical profile figure, bold condensed type overlay, register composition, graphic and monumental"

provenance.notes: Reference: WPA Federal Art Project posters (1930s), Shepard Fairey's stencil work, and the Risograph poster community for stylistic grounding.

egy.techno_hieratic_poster_remix.name: Techno-Hieratic Poster Remix
egy.techno_hieratic_poster_remix.summary: A modern remix overlay that places Egyptian formal visual grammar — registers, hieroglyphic-inspired marks, canonical figures — in a contemporary technical/sci-fi aesthetic context as poster art.
egy.techno_hieratic_poster_remix.description:
This remix applies the "historical-first, remix as overlay" principle: the underlying composition, proportions, and figure canon remain authentically Egyptian; modern technical or sci-fi elements are added as surface layer. Key overlay elements: - Circuit trace patterns replace decorative border bands (following the
  horizontal register rhythm).
- Canonical figures wear both traditional regalia AND technological accessories
  (holographic ankh amulets, integrated circuit crowns, data-glyph cartouches).
- Glowing neon colour fills (electric blue, green, or magenta) overlay the
  canonical mineral pigment zones while maintaining the flat-fill convention.
- Abstract glyph-mark columns use the correct column-narrow layout but employ
  invented tech-inspired marks (circuit symbols, binary patterns in column format).
- The overall composition remains register-structured — the sci-fi elements
  do not break the horizontal band logic.
Output format: contemporary screen-printed or digital poster aesthetic, with bold type (ideally a geometric or Egyptian-revival typeface for labels).

do: Maintain Egyptian register and profile-canon composition as the structural base.
Apply sci-fi/tech elements as overlay on top of correctly proportioned canonical figures.
Label artwork clearly as contemporary artistic invention, not historical reproduction.
Use circuit/tech border elements to replace (not mix with) period-accurate borders.
avoid: Avoid replacing the human/deity figure canon with robotic or non-figure elements.
Avoid fake hieroglyphic texts claiming to be actual Egyptian script.
Avoid disrespectful treatments of sacred themes (Opening of the Mouth, etc.).

egy.techno_hieratic_poster_remix.prompt_fragment: "Egyptian techno-poster remix, canonical profile figures with circuit detail overlay, register layout preserved, neon glow accents on mineral pigment base, hieroglyphic-inspired tech glyph columns, Afrofuturist pharaoh aesthetic, bold poster composition"

provenance.notes: This remix is explicitly a contemporary artistic invention. Reference the Afrofuturism movement and artists like Lina Iris Viktor for respectful high-profile examples of this aesthetic territory.

egy.temple_relief_style.name: Temple Relief Style
egy.temple_relief_style.summary: Carved and pigmented stone relief work found on temple walls, combining sculptural depth with painted colour, spanning Old Kingdom through Ptolemaic periods.
egy.temple_relief_style.description: Temple relief is the monumental public face of Egyptian art. Two techniques dominate: raised relief (figures project above the background) and sunken/sunk relief (figures are carved below the surface, ideal for bright desert sunlight which casts crisp shadows). Both were typically painted after carving. The style is characterised by crisp carved edges, directional side-lighting that reads as line, flat pigment colour zones, and hierarchical composition. Ptolemaic temple reliefs (Edfu, Dendera, Philae) show increased technical complexity with finer detail. The formal register system and composite-profile canon apply throughout.

do: Use directional side-lighting (typically from upper-left) to read carved edges.
Apply flat pigment colour fields within carved contour lines.
Maintain register baseline structure on continuous wall surfaces.
Add weathering (abrasion, dust patina) for historical grounding.
avoid: Avoid soft shadow gradients — keep shadow sharp at carved edges.
Avoid decorative detail that would be unreadable at architectural scale.

egy.temple_relief_style.prompt_fragment: "ancient Egyptian temple relief carving, raised relief, painted stone, directional side-lighting, flat pigment fills, monumental register composition, Ptolemaic temple style, weathered limestone, regal and mythic"

sources: Hawass, Z. (2003). Secrets of the Valley of the Kings. National Geographic.
Robins, G. (1997). The Art of Ancient Egypt. British Museum Press.

egy.tomb_painting_style.name: Egyptian Tomb Painting Style
egy.tomb_painting_style.summary: The canonical flat-colour painted mural style found in New Kingdom rock-cut tombs, characterised by register layouts, composite figures, and mineral pigments on white plaster.
egy.tomb_painting_style.description: Ancient Egyptian tomb painting reached its apex in the New Kingdom (c. 1550–1070 BCE), particularly in the Theban necropolis (Valley of the Kings, Tombs of the Nobles). The style is defined by: a white or cream plaster ground; flat areas of mineral pigment (Egyptian blue, red ochre, yellow ochre, green, black, white) bounded by black ink outlines; figures arranged in horizontal registers with a baseline; the composite-profile canon (frontal torso, profile head and legs); and scale hierarchy where size denotes rank. Backgrounds are typically plain, leaving the emphasis on figures and hieroglyphic captions. Scenes cover daily life, funerary ritual, offerings, and mythological journeys.

do: Use flat, even colour fills bounded by a confident black ink outline.
Organise figures in horizontal baseline registers.
Apply composite-profile canon to all human and divine figures.
Limit palette to the six canonical mineral pigments of the period.
Include a white or cream ground to maximise colour legibility.
avoid: Avoid atmospheric perspective, cast shadows, or volumetric shading.
Avoid photorealistic rendering — flatness is the aesthetic principle.
Avoid mixing unrelated cultural motifs into the same register without remix labelling.

egy.tomb_painting_style.prompt_fragment: "ancient Egyptian tomb painting, flat mineral pigment fills, bold black ink outline, horizontal register composition, white plaster ground, New Kingdom, composite profile figures, solemn funerary atmosphere"

sources: Manniche, L. (1997). Egyptian Art. British Museum Press.
Robins, G. (1997). The Art of Ancient Egypt. British Museum Press.

egy.tomb_red_ochre_palette.name: Tomb Ochre Palette
egy.tomb_red_ochre_palette.summary: The warm earth-toned palette of ochre red, yellow ochre, carbon black, and calcite white — the workhorse colour system of Egyptian tomb painting.
egy.tomb_red_ochre_palette.description: The tomb ochre palette is the everyday colour system of Egyptian funerary wall painting, emphasising warm mineral earths over the more festive gold and lapis tones. It draws on red ochre for male skin and warm accents, yellow ochre for female skin and grounds, carbon black for outlines and detail, and calcite white for garments and highlights. Egyptian blue and malachite green appear as accents for divine colour zones and vegetation, but the dominant warmth is earth-based. This palette reads as grounded, solemn, and historically authentic at a glance. It is the most legible at small scale and in reproduction, making it useful for print and low-resolution contexts. The palette also includes the warm cream of the plaster ground, which glows through thin paint washes.

do: Use red-brown (#B94A2C) for male skin, yellow-ochre (#C8922A) for female skin.
Keep the warm plaster-cream ground visible at borders and thin paint zones.
Add Egyptian blue and malachite green sparingly as divine accents only.
avoid: Avoid cool blue-dominated overall palette — this palette is warm-earth led.
Avoid pure black backgrounds — use warm dark brown for depth.

egy.tomb_red_ochre_palette.prompt_fragment: "Egyptian tomb ochre palette, warm red-brown and yellow ochre, male and female skin tones, carbon black outline, white plaster ground, solemn and earthy, ancient Egyptian wall painting"

sources: Lee, L. & Quirke, S. (2000). 'Painting materials.' In Nicholson & Shaw (eds.), Ancient Egyptian Materials and Technology.

egy.uraeus_cobra.name: Uraeus Cobra
egy.uraeus_cobra.summary: The rearing Egyptian cobra — emblem of divine royal authority, fire, and protection — worn on the headdress of pharaohs and deities, and placed atop crowns and diadems.
egy.uraeus_cobra.description: The uraeus (from Greek ouraios, possibly from Egyptian iaret, "the rearing one") is the stylised rearing Egyptian cobra (Naja naja or Naja haje), depicted upright with hood spread and body coiled or looped behind. It is the emblem of the serpent goddess Wadjet of Buto (Lower Egypt) and represents the solar fire that destroys the pharaoh's enemies. It is most commonly shown attached to the front of royal crowns and headdresses (White Crown, Red Crown, Blue Crown, Nemes headdress) as the royal diadem element. Deities also wear the uraeus. Pairs of uraei flank the winged sun disc. Triple uraei appear on some divine headdresses. The uraeus is depicted with naturalistically curled hood, occasionally with solar disc on head, and in gold or polychrome faience. Its distinctive rearing silhouette is instantly recognisable as a royal/divine identifier.

do: Show in rearing pose with spread cobra hood — not coiled or lying flat.
Attach to crown or headdress brow for royal/divine figures.
Depict hood with ribbed or cross-hatched detail for scale texture.
avoid: Avoid naturalistic snake poses (coiled, hunting) — the rearing upright form is canonical.
Avoid placing uraeus on non-royal, non-divine figures without specific mythological context.

egy.uraeus_cobra.prompt_fragment: "uraeus cobra, Egyptian royal serpent, rearing cobra with spread hood, gold and faience, crown diadem element, divine protection emblem, regal and solemn, ancient Egypt"

sources: Wilkinson, R.H. (1992). Reading Egyptian Art. Thames and Hudson.
Wilkinson, R.H. (2003). The Complete Gods and Goddesses of Ancient Egypt.

egy.was_scepter.name: Was Scepter
egy.was_scepter.summary: The animal-headed staff symbol of divine power and dominion, carried by gods and pharaohs as an emblem of authority over sky, earth, and underworld.
egy.was_scepter.description: The was scepter is a long staff with a distinctive canid animal head at the top (resembling the Seth animal or a stylised dog/jackal) and a forked base that rests on the ground. The hieroglyphic sign (Gardiner S40) carries the meaning "power" or "dominion." In tomb and temple art, was scepters are carried by virtually all major deities — Amun, Ra, Thoth, Hathor — often alongside the ankh (in the other hand) or the djed pillar. The pharaoh's throne may rest on a was sign. The staff appears in triadic group formulas (ankh + djed + was = life + stability + power) carved on furniture, coffins, and architectural elements. The animal head shape distinguishes it from the simpler heqa crook scepter.

do: Show the distinctive canid animal head at the top with upright ears.
Include a forked or bifurcated base foot — essential identifying feature.
Typically gold-yellow or paired with teal/green staff colour.
avoid: Avoid confusing with the heqa crook — the was is straight with an animal head.
Avoid generic staff designs without the canid head and forked base.

sources: Wilkinson, R.H. (1992). Reading Egyptian Art. Thames and Hudson.
Wilkinson, R.H. (2003). The Complete Gods and Goddesses of Ancient Egypt. Thames and Hudson.

egy.winged_sun_disc.name: Winged Sun Disc
egy.winged_sun_disc.summary: The solar disc flanked by spread falcon wings — an ancient emblem of divine kingship, solar power, and celestial protection displayed above temple doorways.
egy.winged_sun_disc.description: The winged sun disc (Egyptian: Behdety) represents Horus of Behdet, a solar hawk deity, and by extension the divine power of the sun and the pharaoh. In its canonical form: a central red-brown or gold sun disc, flanked by two spread falcon wings (coloured in banded feather patterns of blue, green, and ochre), and often flanked by two erect cobras (uraeus) wearing the crowns of Upper and Lower Egypt. It appears above virtually every temple doorway and entrance as an apotropaic emblem, on the lintels of naos shrines, on coffin lids, and on royal pectorals. The form is among the most architectural of Egyptian motifs — it functions as a horizontal capstone element. The Assyrians, Persians, and other Near Eastern cultures adopted similar winged-disc iconography, reflecting Egyptian cultural influence.

do: Centre the disc on a bilateral axis — the wings must be symmetric.
Include banded feather detail on both wings.
Include paired uraeus cobras flanking the disc where historically accurate.
Use above doorways/lintels as architectural capstone element.
avoid: Avoid asymmetric wing poses — symmetry is structurally essential to this emblem.
Avoid omitting the disc — wings alone without centre disc lose the solar identity.

sources: Wilkinson, R.H. (1992). Reading Egyptian Art. Thames and Hudson.
Quirke, S. & Spencer, J. (1992). The British Museum Book of Ancient Egypt.
